claims.text: Equimolar CuMoTaWV can be fabricated as a refractory high-entropy alloy thin film by DC magnetron sputtering.
The CuMoTaWV film can be deposited on silicon or 304 stainless-steel substrates.
The as-deposited CuMoTaWV film has a nanocrystalline BCC solid-solution structure.
Nanocrystalline CuMoTaWV films possess high hardness and compressive strength.
Post-deposition annealing under a tuned oxygen partial pressure will create a continuous nanoscale oxide surface layer on CuMoTaWV.
The annealing-induced oxide layer will be stable over the intended operating-temperature range.
Oxides of tungsten, tantalum, or copper formed on the alloy will act as lubricious phases.
The engineered oxide layer will reduce surface friction through inherent lubrication.
Selective surface oxidation will decouple tribological performance from the mechanical properties of the bulk alloy.
The refractory high-entropy alloy beneath the oxide layer will retain its high hardness and strength after oxygen-controlled annealing.
The annealed, oxide-bearing film will have a significantly lower coefficient of friction than an untreated CuMoTaWV film.
The annealed, oxide-bearing film will have a significantly lower wear rate than an untreated CuMoTaWV film.
The friction and wear benefits will persist from room temperature to at least 300 degrees Celsius.
The tribological improvement will occur without a noticeable loss of mechanical strength.
Untreated RHEA films combine high mechanical strength with relatively high friction and wear under extreme-temperature conditions.
HEA coatings on lower-cost substrates are a potentially economical approach for harsh-environment applications.
The proposed approach is primarily applicable to thin-film coatings.
Performance may be limited when the lubricious oxide becomes unstable beyond the tested temperature or environmental range.
Optimal annealing conditions and oxygen partial pressure depend on alloy composition and operating conditions.
